## 6. Metric embeddings of path spaces into dense subsets of path spaces

In this section we prove Theorem 1.2. We restate the theorem below with explicit constants.

#### Theorem 6.1 (Metric embeddings of paths into dense subsets of paths).

For all $k\geqslant 3,0<\delta<1,0<\varepsilon\leqslant 1$ , we have:

$$ e^{0.1k\log(1/\delta)}\leqslant Path(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k)\leqslant e^{100k\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)}. $$

The proof of the upper bound is similar to the proof in [14]. We use a porosity argument. We show that for any interval $I$ , if $\mathcal{D}\cap I$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$ -distorted copy of $[k]$ then $\mathcal{D}\cap I$ is disjoint from an interval $I^{\prime}\subset I$ of diameter $\asymp\varepsilon|I|/k$ . This is the discrete analogue of a porous set in geometric measure theory. It is well-known that porous sets do not have full Hausdorff dimension (e.g. see Chapter 11 in the book [29]), and our argument mimics this fact. The lower bound follows from a Cantor set construction. We construct $\mathcal{D}\subset[N]$ by removing the middle $4N/k$ -sized interval $I$ of $[N]$ at each iteration. We argue that for any $(1+\varepsilon)$ -bi-Lipschitz map $f:[k]\to\mathcal{D}$ , the image of $f$ must lie entirely in only one of the two subintervals of $[N]-I$ , and continue recursively.

### 6.1. Upper bound (via a porosity argument)

#### Proof.

Throughout the proof, we will fix $N\in\mathbb{N}$ which is sufficiently large, and $\mathcal{D}\subset[N]$ which has density $\delta\in(0,1)$ (i.e. $|\mathcal{D}|\geqslant\delta N$ ). We will assume that there does not exist a $(1+\varepsilon)$ bi-Lipschitz embedding $f:[k]\to\mathcal{D}$ , and our goal is to prove an upper bound on the size $|\mathcal{D}|$ .

Step 1: A single induction step: Consider the $k$ equidistant points $p_{1},\ldots,p_{k}$ in the middle thirds subinterval of $N$ .

$$ p_{i}:=i\dfrac{N}{3k}+\dfrac{N}{3}\;\;\;\text{for all }i=1,...,k. $$

For simplicity of notation we will ignore any floor functions in this section. Consider now the interval centered at $p_{1},...,p_{k}$ of small diameter:

$$ I_{i}:=[p_{i}-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}N,p_{i}+\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}N]\;\;\;\text{for all }i=1,...,k. $$

It is routine to check that any map $f:[k]\to[N]$ with $f(i)\in I_{i}$ for all $i=1,...,k$ is a $(1+\varepsilon)$ bi-Lipschitz embedding of the path space $[k]$ . By the hypothesis on $\mathcal{D}$ this means that for some $i\in[k]$ , $I_{i}\cap\mathcal{D}=\emptyset$ . We can therefore write $[N]-I_{i}=I^{0}\cup I^{1}$ where $I^{0},I^{1}$ are disjoint intervals of diameter $>N/3$ . (Note that we removed an interval of density $\asymp\varepsilon/k$ and not an interval of density $\asymp 1/k$ . This is important in the estimate of Step 4.) This completes the base case in the induction.

Step 2: Iterating the inductive step: We now apply the same argument to $I^{0}\cap\mathcal{D}\subset I^{0}$ and $I^{1}\cap\mathcal{D}\subset I^{1}$ . We pick $k$ equidistant points on the middle thirds subinterval of $I^{0}$ and place intervals of radius $\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}|I^{0}|$ at each point. By the hypothesis, one of these intervals is disjoint from $\mathcal{D}$ . This means that $\mathcal{D}\cap I^{0}$ lies in the union of two disjoint subintervals $I^{00}$ and $I^{01}$ each of diameter $>N/9$ .

Step 3: Estimating the total number of iterations: We apply this argument $M:=\log_{3}(N/3k)$ times. Observe that after $M$ iterations, every interval has at least $k$ points and therefore we have enough points to pick $p_{1},...,p_{k}$ and the intervals $I_{1},...,I_{k}$ in the next iteration.

Step 4: Estimating the size of $\mathcal{D}$ : At the $m^{\text{th}}$ -iteration for each $m=1,...,M$ , we conclude that the set $\mathcal{D}$ lies inside the union of $2^{m}$ intervals. Denote this union by $U_{m}$ . Because we remove a large subinterval from each interval in the $m^{\text{th}}$ -iteration, we have $|U_{m+1}|\leqslant(1-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k})|U_{m}|$ . We conclude:

$$ |\mathcal{D}|\leqslant|U_{M}|\leqslant\left(1-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}\right)^{M}N=\left(1-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}\right)^{-\log_{3}(3k)}\left(1-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}\right)^{\log_{3}N}N=\left(1-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}\right)^{-\log_{3}(3k)}N^{1+\log_{3}(1-\varepsilon/18k)}. $$

Since for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have $(1-1/m)^{m}\geqslant 1/4$ , we have

$$ \left(1-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{18k}\right)^{-\log_{3}(3k)}\leqslant 4^{(\varepsilon/18k)\log_{3}(3k)}=\exp\left[\left(\dfrac{\log 4}{18\log 3}\right)\dfrac{\varepsilon\log k}{k}\right]\leqslant e^{\varepsilon\log k/10k}. $$

Next, by the concavity of the logarithm at $1$ :

$$ \log_{3}(1-\varepsilon/18k)<-\dfrac{1}{18\ln 3}\dfrac{\varepsilon}{k}<-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{50k} $$

Rearranging the terms in the inequality, we get:

$$ \delta\leqslant|\mathcal{D}|/N\leqslant e^{\varepsilon\log k/10k}N^{-\varepsilon/50k}\iff N^{-\varepsilon/50k}\leqslant\dfrac{1}{\delta}\;e^{\varepsilon\log k/10k} $$

$$ \iff\log N\leqslant\dfrac{50k}{\varepsilon}\left(\log(1/\delta)+\dfrac{\varepsilon\log k}{10k}\right)=50\dfrac{k\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}+10\log k<100\dfrac{k\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}. $$

∎

### 6.2. Lower bound (via a Cantor set construction)

#### Proof.

Step 1: Construction of the Cantor set. Throughout the proof we will fix $N\in\mathbb{N}$ which is sufficiently large, and construct a sequence of finer and finer approximations $[N]=U_{0}\supset U_{1}\supset...\supset U_{M}=:\mathcal{D}$ . For each $m=1,...,M$ , $U_{m}$ will be the disjoint union of $2^{m}$ intervals. At the first step, we divide $[N]=I^{0}\cup I^{mid}\cup I^{1}$ where

$$ I^{0}:=[1,N(1/2-2/k)],\;\;\;I^{mid}:=[N(1/2-2/k),N(1/2+2/k)]\;\;\;I^{1}:=[N(1/2+2/k),N], $$

and set $U_{1}:=I^{0}\cup I^{1}$ . In plain words, we remove the middle interval of length $(4/k)N$ . At the second step, we remove the middle interval of length $(4/k)|I^{0}|$ from $I^{0}$ to obtain $I^{00},I^{01}$ and do the same for $I^{1}$ and set $U_{2}:=I^{00}\cup I^{01}\cup I^{10}\cup I^{11}$ . At the $m^{\text{th}}$ step, we take each of the $2^{m}$ intervals of $U_{m}$ and remove in each the middle interval of density $4/k$ to obtain $U_{m+1}$ . Observe that each interval in $U_{m}$ has diameter $<(2/3)^{m}N$ . We iterate this construction $M=\log_{3/2}(N)$ steps, which ensures that the $2^{M}$ intervals which comprise $U_{M}$ are all singletons.

Step 2: Analysis to forbid an embedding at a single scale Claim: if $f:[k]\to I^{0}\cup I^{1}$ has distortion $\leqslant 2$ , then either $f([k])\subset I^{0}$ or else $f([k])\subset I^{1}$ . Suppose not. Then there exists $i\in[k]$ such that $f(i)\in I^{0}$ while $f(i+1)\in I^{1}$ . This implies that $|f(i)-f(i+1)|>4N/k=4N/k|i-(i+1)|$ . On the other hand, either $I^{0}$ or $I^{1}$ , say $I^{0}$ has $|f([k])\cap I^{0}|\geqslant k/2$ . By pigeonholing (cover $I^{0}$ with $k/2$ balls of radius $N/k$ each), there exists $j\neq j^{\prime}\in[k]$ such that $|f(j)-f(j^{\prime})|\leqslant 2N/k\leqslant 2N/k|j-j^{\prime}|$ . We obtain the distortion bound:

$$ Distortion(f)\geqslant\dfrac{|f(i)-f(i+1)|/|i-(i+1)|}{|f(j)-f(j^{\prime})|/|j-j^{\prime}|}>\dfrac{4N/k}{2N/k}=2 $$

and the claim follows. Similarly, we can apply this claim to any interval in the Cantor set construction. For every $m=1,...,M$ and any $\alpha\in\{0,1\}^{m}$ if we have an embedding $f:[k]\to I^{\alpha 0}\cup I^{\alpha 1}$ with distortion $\leqslant 2$ , then either $f([k])\subset I^{\alpha 0}$ or else $f([k])\subset I^{\alpha 1}$ .

Step 3: Recursive argument to forbid any embedding: Suppose that $f:[k]\to\mathcal{D}$ has distortion $\leqslant 2$ . Since $\mathcal{D}\subset I^{0}\cup I^{1}$ , by the above claim, either $f([k])\subset I^{0}$ or else $f([k])\subset I^{1}$ . Denote by $I^{\alpha_{1}}$ this interval. By the same reasoning, since $\mathcal{D}\cap I^{\alpha_{1}}\subset I^{\alpha_{1}0}\cup I^{\alpha_{1}1}$ , either $f([k])\subset I^{\alpha_{1}0}$ or else $f([k])\subset I^{\alpha_{1}1}$ . Denote this interval by $I^{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}$ . By iteratively applying the claim $M$ -times, we conclude that $f([k])\subset I^{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha\in\{0,1\}^{M}$ . However, by construction $I^{\alpha}$ has diameter $<N(2/3)^{M}=1$ meaning that $I^{\alpha}$ is a singleton. A $2$ -bi-Lipschitz map must be a bijection so we arrive at a contradiction.

Step 4: Estimating the size of $\mathcal{D}$ : We now prove a lower bound on the size of the Cantor set $\mathcal{D}$ . We have: $N=|U_{0}|$ and $|U_{m+1}|=(1-4/k)|U_{m}|$ so we get:

$$ \delta N:=|\mathcal{D}|=(1-4/k)^{M}N=N^{1+\ln(1-4/k)/\ln(3/2)}>N^{1-(4/\ln(3/2))(1/k)} $$

where at the last step we used the concavity of the logarithm.

Rearranging the terms, we get: $N\geqslant e^{C^{\prime}k\log(1/\delta)}$ where $C^{\prime}=\ln(3/2)/4$ . ∎

## 7. Metric embeddings of binary trees into dense subsets of binary trees

In this section we prove Theorem 1.3. We restate the theorem below with explicit constants.

#### Theorem 7.1 (Metric embeddings of trees into dense subsets of trees).

For all $k\geqslant 3,0<\delta<1,0<\varepsilon\leqslant 0.001$ , we have:

$$ e^{0.1k\log(1/\delta)}\leqslant Tree(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k)\leqslant e^{1000k\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)}. $$

The upper bound uses as black boxes the upper bound for path spaces in Theorem 1.2 and the Ramsey theorem for tree replicas of Pach–Solymosi–Tardos (namely Theorem 1 in [40]), and the rest of the proof is analogous to the proof of the Furstenberg–Weiss theorem in [40]. The lower bound uses the same Cantor set construction as in the lower bound of Theorem 1.2, along with a characterization of path embeddings $[k]\to Tree(N)$ of small distortion.

### 7.1. Upper bound (via the tree replicas theorem of Pach–Solymosi–Tardos)

We first recall some terminology about binary trees from [40]. Let $N^{\prime},N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $N^{\prime}\leqslant N$ .

A tree replica is a map $f:Tree(N^{\prime})\to Tree(N)$ which satisfies two properties. –First, if $w_{1},w_{2}\in Tree(N^{\prime})$ which lie on the same level of the tree $Tree(N^{\prime})$ , i.e. $l(w_{1})=l(w_{2})$ , then $f(w_{1})$ and $f(w_{2})$ lie in the same level of the tree $Tree(N)$ , i.e. $l(f(w_{1}))=l(f(w_{2}))$ . –Secondly, for all $w\in Tree(N^{\prime})$ with immediate children $w_{0}$ and $w_{1}$ , if we denote by $f(w)_{0}$ and $f(w)_{1}$ the immediate children of $f(w)$ , then $f(w_{0})$ is a descendant of $f(w)_{0}$ and $f(w_{1})$ is a descendant of $f(w)_{1}$ (in vague words, the image of the tree ”branches out” immediately after each point).

In [40], Pach–Solymosi–Tardos proved the following Ramsey theorem about tree replicas (Theorem 1). They combined their result with Szemerédi’s theorem to give quantitative bounds on the Furstenberg–Weiss theorem. Denote by $h:[0,1/2]\to[0,1]$ the Shannon binary entropy function

$$ h(p):=p\log(1/p)+(1-p)\log(1/(1-p)). $$

#### Theorem 7.2 (Pach–Solymosi–Tardos).

For all $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0<\delta<1$ , any subset $\mathcal{D}\subset Tree(N)$ with $\mu(\mathcal{D})\geqslant\delta$ contains an arithmetic tree replica $f:Tree(N^{\prime})\to\mathcal{D}$ with $N^{\prime}\geqslant\lfloor h^{-1}(\delta)N\rfloor$ .

#### Proof.

We are given $\mathcal{D}\subset Tree(N)$ with $\mu(\mathcal{D})\geqslant\delta$ . By Theorem 7.2 we obtain a tree replica: $f:Tree(N^{\prime})\to\mathcal{D}$ where $N^{\prime}:=h^{-1}(\delta)N$ .

Similar to [40], we now consider the set of possible levels of $f(Tree(N^{\prime}))\subset\mathcal{D}$ . Call this set $\mathcal{D}_{path}\subset[N]$ , and observe that it has density $|\mathcal{D}_{path}|/N=h^{-1}(\delta)$ . By the upper bound of Theorem 1.2, we can find an $\varepsilon$ -distorted copy of the path $[k]$ sitting inside $\mathcal{D}_{path}$ so long as:

$$ N\leqslant e^{100k\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/h^{-1}(\delta))}\leqslant e^{1000k\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)}. $$

In the last inequality, we used the quantitative bound (and took the logarithm):

$$ h^{-1}(\delta)\geqslant\delta^{2}\;\;\;\text{for all }0\leqslant\delta\leqslant 1/2 $$

We consider only the levels of $Tree(N^{\prime})$ which map one of the $k$ levels of the path $[k]$ in $\mathcal{D}_{path}$ . This gives us a map $f^{\prime}:Tree(k)\to\mathcal{D}$ which is an $\varepsilon$ -distorted embedding. ∎

### 7.2. Lower bound (via stability of path metrics in trees)

We first describe the $\delta$ -dense subset of the tree which avoids tree copies. The description is much easier than the analysis. Let $\mathcal{D}_{path}\subset[N]$ be the Cantor set which was constructed in subsection 6.2. We take $\mathcal{D}\subset Tree(N)$ to be the set of all points $w\in Tree(N)$ whose level $l(w)$ lies in this set $\mathcal{D}_{path}$ . Clearly, $\mu(\mathcal{D})=\mu(\mathcal{D}_{path})$ . The lower bound follows once we show that $Tree(k)$ cannot embed into $\mathcal{D}$ with small distortion. In fact, we will show something stronger: the path metric space $[k]$ cannot embed into $\mathcal{D}$ with small distortion.

Recall that a geodesic in a graph is a shortest path between two points (which is always unique in a tree). A geodesic between $w,w^{\prime}\in Tree(N)$ has a very special form: the geodesic starts at $w$ , travels upward the tree until the least common ancestor $w\vee w^{\prime}$ of $w$ and $w^{\prime}$ is visited, and then moves downwards again to $w^{\prime}$ . We need the following stability lemma:

#### Lemma 7.3 (Every small distortion path in a tree is close to a geodesic).

If $f:[k]\to Tree(N)$ is a $0.001$ -distorted embedding with rescaling $r\in[N]$ , and $\gamma\subset Tree(N)$ is the geodesic from $f(1)$ to $f(k)$ in $Tree(N)$ , then every point in the image of $f$ is close to $\gamma$ :

$$ d_{T}(f(i),\gamma):=\min_{w\in\gamma}d_{T}(f(i),w)\leqslant 0.001r\;\;\;\text{for all }i\in[k]. $$

#### Proof.

Step 1: notation for tripods in trees: Given any triple of points $w,w^{\prime},w^{\prime\prime}\in Tree(N)$ we can form a tripod which is the union of all the geodesics $w\to w^{\prime}$ , $w^{\prime}\to w^{\prime\prime}$ and $w\to w^{\prime\prime}$ . Because of the tree structure, this tripod consists of a median point $m$ such that each of the $3$ geodesics must pass through $m$ (e.g. the geodesic $w\to w^{\prime}$ is the geodesic $w\to m$ concatenated by the geodesic $m\to w^{\prime}$ ). Step 2: tripods of $3$ consecutive points must be degenerate: For each $i\in[k-2]$ consider the points $f(i),f(i+1),f(i+2)$ and form their tripod. Denote the median by $g(i+1)$ . We claim that because $f(i),f(i+1),f(i+2)$ form a slightly distorted copy of the path of length $3$ , this forces $f(i+1)$ and $g(i+1)$ to be very close to each other. In particular, we have the estimates:

$$ d_{T}(f(i),f(i+2))=d_{T}(f(i),g(i+1))+d_{T}(g(i+1),f(i+2))\geqslant 2r $$

$$ d_{T}(f(i),f(i+1))=d_{T}(f(i),g(i+1))+d_{T}(g(i+1),f(i+1))\leqslant(1.001)r $$

$$ d_{T}(f(i+1),f(i+2))=d_{T}(f(i+1),g(i+1))+d_{T}(g(i+1),f(i+2))\leqslant(1.001)r $$

adding the last two inequalities and subtracting the first, we get:

$$ 2d_{T}(f(i+1),g(i+1))\leqslant 0.002r\implies d_{T}(f(i+1),g(i+1))\leqslant 0.001r. $$

Step 3: gluing all the tripods together: Set $g(1):=f(1)$ and $g(k):=f(k)$ .

#### Claim 7.4.

For all $i\in[k-2]$ , the geodesic from $g(i)$ to $g(i+2)$ must pass through the point $g(i+1)$

#### Proof.

This is a tedious routine check. Recall that by definition, both $g(i)$ and $g(i+1)$ belong to the unique geodesic from $f(i)\to f(i+1)$ and both $g(i+1)$ and $g(i+2)$ belong to the unique geodesic from $f(i+1)\to f(i+2)$ . Consider the geodesics from $g(i)\to f(i+1)$ and from $g(i+2)\to f(i+1)$ , and let $m$ be the first common point (i.e. $m$ is the median of the tripod formed by $\{g(i),g(i+2),f(i+1)\}$ ). The path joining the geodesics from $f(i)\to g(i)\to m\to g(i+2)\to f(i+2)$ is also a geodesic and since $g(i+1)$ is the median of the tripod formed by $\{f(i),f(i+1),f(i+2)\}$ it must be the case that $m=g(i+1)$ . This shows the claim. ∎

Applying the above claim we conclude that the path $\gamma$ from $f(1)=g(1)\to g(2)\to...\to g(k)=f(k)$ is a geodesic from $f(1)$ to $f(k)$ . (If not, then there exists an edge in the tree which is crossed for two consecutive times. Because the path is a union of geodesics, this event can only happen when the edge is crossed at the end of a geodesic from $g(i)\to g(i+1)$ and then the same edge is crossed again at the beginning of the geodesic from $g(i+1)\to g(i+2)$ . This contradicts the lemma, because in that event the geodesic from $g(i)\to g(i+2)$ does not pass through $g(i+1)$ .) Together with the bound 49 we get the desired conclusion. ∎

We are now in a position to prove the lower bound in Theorem 1.3.

#### Proof.

Suppose $f:[k]\to Tree(N)$ is an embedding of distortion $<0.001$ . Then by the above lemma, we take the geodesic from $f(1)$ to $f(k)$ and conclude that each point in the image, say $f(i)$ is $0.01r$ -close to a point on the geodesic $g(i)$ . By the remark made earlier, half of the geodesic is level-decreasing and the other half is level increasing. One of the two pieces must have at least $k/2$ of the points $g(1),...,g(k)$ . Without loss of generality say it is the first half of the path, so $g(1),g(2),...,g(k/2)$ is level decreasing. It is a little tedious but not hard to check that the set of levels $\{l(f(1)),...,l(f(k/2))\}\subset[N]$ forms a $2$ -distorted path of length $k/2$ in $[N]$ . By the lower bound of Theorem 1.2 this forces $N$ to be large:

$$ N\geqslant Path(2,\delta,k/2)=e^{\Omega(k\log(1/\delta))}. $$

∎

## 8. Large subsets of the Hamming cube have trivial BMW type

In order to prove Theorem 1.4 we will use the following variation of Theorem 1.1.

#### Theorem 8.1.

There exist universal constants $c,c^{\prime}>0$ such that for all $0<\gamma<1$ and $N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $N\geqslant c\gamma^{-3/2}$ , If $\mathcal{D}\subset Q_{N}$ has size $|\mathcal{D}|>2^{(1-\gamma)N}$ , then $\mathcal{D}$ contains a $2$ -distorted copy of the Hamming cube of dimension $\geqslant c^{\prime}/\sqrt{\gamma}$ .

#### Proof.

We will denote by $k\in\mathbb{N}$ the dimension of the Hamming cube we wish to embed. We will need another error parameter $0<\varepsilon_{3}<1$ (not to be confused with the error terms $\varepsilon_{1}$ and $\varepsilon_{2}$ in Theorem 4.11).

Step 1: Inflating the set $\mathcal{D}$ by $\varepsilon_{3}$ to reach density $1/2$ : We will inflate the set $\mathcal{D}$ by an error $\varepsilon_{3}\asymp 1/k$ to cover $1/2$ of the density and then we will apply Theorem 4.11 to argue that $\mathcal{D}$ is close to a roughly equitable block copy. Suppose that $|\mathcal{D}|\geqslant|Ball(pN)|$ for some $0<p<1$ . By Harper’s inequality (Lemma 4.3), if $pN+\varepsilon_{3}N>N/2$ then $\mu(\mathcal{D}_{\varepsilon_{3}})>1/2$ , which is what we desire. We need to estimate, for all $0<\gamma<1$ , the largest value of $p$ such that

$$ |\mathcal{D}|\geqslant 2^{(1-\gamma)N}>|Ball(pN)|. $$

We apply the Hoeffding’s bounds (Lemma 4.1) with $\varepsilon=\sqrt{2\ln(2)\gamma}$ to get:

$$ \left|Ball\left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{2\ln(2)\;\gamma}}{2}N\right)\right|\leqslant 2^{N}e^{-(2\ln(2)\gamma)(N/2)}=2^{(1-\gamma)N}. $$

We take $\varepsilon_{3}:=\sqrt{\ln(2)\gamma/2}$ . Harper’s inequality and the bound (50) give us: $\mu(\mathcal{D}_{\varepsilon_{3}})\geqslant 1/2$ . We choose the largest $k$ such that $\varepsilon_{3}<1/1000k$ , i.e. $k=\lfloor\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1000\sqrt{\ln 2}}\gamma^{-1/2}\rfloor+1$ .

Step 2: Finding a roughly equitable block copy of large rescaling: By Theorem 4.11 with $\varepsilon=1/2$ and $\delta=1/2$ we get a roughly equitable block copy with block error $\varepsilon_{1}=1/100$ and rescaling $r=N/2k(1-\varepsilon_{1}-4\varepsilon_{2}k)$ inside the twice-inflated set $\mathcal{D}_{\varepsilon_{3}+\varepsilon_{2}}$ , where $\varepsilon_{2}=1/1000k$ . Written in the notation of section 4.1, we have: $\mathcal{V}_{\pm\varepsilon_{1}}^{k,n}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}}\bigr)\neq\emptyset$ . Applying Proposition 4.10 with perturbation error $\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}\leqslant 1/(100k)$ and block error $\varepsilon_{1}=1/100$ , conclude that $\mathcal{D}$ contains a $10$ -distorted copy of the Hamming cube $Q_{k}$ of dimension $k\gtrsim 1/\sqrt{\gamma}$ and the proof is complete. ∎

We state and prove the contrapositive of Theorem 1.4 since it is more convenient for the logic of the proof.

#### Theorem 8.2 (Rewritten - large subsets of the Hamming cube have trivial BMW type).

There are universal constants $c,c^{\prime}>0$ such that the following holds. For any $\gamma>0$ and $N\geqslant c\gamma^{-3/2}$ and any subset $\mathcal{D}\subset\{0,1\}^{N}$ of size $|\mathcal{D}|\geqslant 2^{(1-\gamma)N}$ we have:

$$ c_{M}(\mathcal{D})\geqslant c^{\prime}T_{p}(M)^{-1}\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{1}{p})} $$

for any metric space $M$ of BMW type $p>1$ constant $T_{p}(M)$ .

#### Proof.

By an argument of Enflo [15, 16] for any metric space $M$ and any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , every map $f:Q_{k}\to M$ has bi-Lipschitz distortion $\geqslant k^{1-1/p}/T_{p}(M)$ . Therefore the theorem follows once we embed $Q_{k}\to\mathcal{D}$ with distortion $<2$ for some $k\gtrsim 1/\sqrt{\gamma}$ . This is precisely the content of Theorem 8.1. ∎

## 9. Union problems for metric type and universality and related remarks

The Hales–Jewett theorem [24] states that for every finite alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ and number of colors $r\in\mathbb{N}$ there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that every $r$ -coloring of the set $\mathcal{A}^{N}$ contains a monochromatic combinatorial line. A combinatorial line is given via $\{l(a):a\in\mathcal{A}\}$ where $l$ is a variable word of length $N$ , i.e. $l\in(\mathcal{A}\cup\{v\})^{N}$ where $v$ is an extra letter which appears at least once in $l$ , and $l(i)\in\mathcal{A}^{N}$ is the word obtained by substituting $i$ in place of the extra letter $v$ .

The density Hales–Jewett theorem of Furstenberg–Katznelson [19] states that for every finite alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ and $\delta>0$ there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that every subset $\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{A}^{N}$ of density $\mu(\mathcal{D}):=|\mathcal{D}|/|\mathcal{A}|^{N}>\delta$ contains a combinatorial line. The multi-dimensional density Hales–Jewett theorem (which follows from the density Hales–Jewett theorem) extracts from dense subsets of $\mathcal{A}^{N}$ a combinatorial subspace which is given by substituting a variable word in multiple variable letters $v_{1},...,v_{k}$ (where each variable letter appears at least once). Observe that combinatorial subspaces do not give metric embeddings $f:\mathcal{A}^{k}\to\mathcal{A}^{N}$ because one variable letter in $v_{1},...,v_{k}$ might have a large number of frequencies in $l$ while another variable letter might have a small number of frequencies in $l$ . See the monograph [11] and the survey [13] for more on the density Hales–Jewett theorem, its variations, and its history.

#### Remark 9.1.

From the density Hales–Jewett theorem, it follows easily that $\Emb(1,\delta,k)<\infty$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0<\delta<1$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0<\delta<1$ and $N$ which will be chosen later. Let $\mathcal{D}\subset Q_{N}$ be a subset of density $\mu(\mathcal{D})\geqslant\delta$ . We break a point $x\in Q_{N}$ into $N/k$ -many blocks of size $k$ , meaning that we view $\mathcal{D}\subset Q_{N}=\mathcal{A}^{N/k}$ where our alphabet is $\mathcal{A}:=Q_{k}$ . Clearly, $\mathcal{D}$ is a subset of density $\delta$ and $|\mathcal{A}|=2^{k}$ . Let $N^{\prime}$ be the dimension from the density Hales–Jewett theorem and choose $N:=kN^{\prime}$ . By the density Hales–Jewett theorem there exists a 1-variable word $l\in(\mathcal{A}\cup\{v\})^{N}$ such that $l(\alpha)\in\mathcal{D}$ for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{A}=Q_{k}$ . Observe $f:\alpha\mapsto l(\alpha)$ gives us a rescaled isometric embedding into $\mathcal{D}$ and the rescaling $r$ is equal to the frequency of the variable letter $v$ in the variable word $l$ . ∎

The same proof works for any $l_{p}$ -grid $([m]^{n},||\cdot||_{p})$ with fixed thickness $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and growing dimension $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . It also gives following lemma which we need to prove Propositions 1.5 and 1.7.

#### Lemma 9.2 (Consequence of the Hales–Jewett theorem).

For each $k,m\in\mathbb{N}$ there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N>n$ the following is true: (1) For any $2$ -coloring (i.e. partition into $2$ pieces) of the Hamming cube $(Q_{N},||\cdot||_{1})$ there exists an isometric embedding with arbitrary rescaling

$$ f:(Q_{k},||\cdot||_{1})\to(Q_{N},||\cdot||_{1}) $$

such that the image $f(Q_{k})$ is monochromatic. (2) For any $2$ -coloring (i.e. partition into $2$ pieces) of the $l_{\infty}$ -grid $([m]^{N},||\cdot||_{\infty})$ there exists an isometric embedding with arbitrary rescaling

$$ f:([m]^{k},||\cdot||_{\infty})\to([m]^{N},||\cdot||_{\infty}) $$

such that the image $f([m]^{k})$ is monochromatic.

#### Proof.

We show only part $(2)$ . Part $(1)$ follows from an identical argument (or alternatively from Remark 9.1). We break a point $x\in[m]^{N}$ into $N/k$ -many blocks of size $k$ , meaning that we view $[m]^{N}=\mathcal{A}^{N/k}$ where our alphabet is $\mathcal{A}:=[m]^{k}$ . Clearly, the $2$ -coloring of $[m]^{N}$ gives us a $2$ -coloring of $\mathcal{A}^{N/k}$ and our alphabet size is $|\mathcal{A}|=m^{k}$ . Let $N^{\prime}$ be the dimension from the Hales–Jewett theorem and choose $N:=kN^{\prime}$ . By the Hales–Jewett theorem, there exists a monochromatic 1-variable word $l\in(\mathcal{A}\cup\{v\})^{N}$ such that $l(\alpha)$ has the same color for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{A}=Q_{k}$ . Observe $f:[m]^{k}\to[m]^{N}:\alpha\mapsto l(\alpha)$ gives us a monochromatic rescaled isometric embedding and the rescaling $r$ is equal to the frequency of the variable letter $v$ in the variable word $l$ . ∎

Next, we prove Proposition 1.5, Proposition 1.6, and Proposition 1.7. We repeat the statements for the convenience of the reader.

#### Proposition 9.3 (The union of metric subspaces of nontrivial BMW type has nontrivial BMW type).

If $(M,d)$ is a metric space with $M=A\cup B$ for some $A,B\subset M$ then

$$ p_{A}>1\;\;\text{and}\;\;p_{B}>1\implies p_{M}>1. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose that $p_{M}=1$ . We will show that either $p_{A}=1$ or else $p_{B}=1$ .

By a theorem of Bourgain–Milman–Wolfson, namely Theorem 2.6 in [8], $p_{M}=1$ if and only if for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , the Hamming cube of dimension $n$ embeds into $M$ with distortion $<1+\varepsilon$ .

For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $n$ be the value from Part (1) of Lemma 9.2. Consider the $2$ -distorted copy $f:Q_{n}\to M$ , and label each point $\alpha\in Q_{n}$ by $A$ if $f(\alpha)\in A$ and by $B$ if $f(\alpha)\in B$ . By Lemma 9.2, we have a monochromatic undistorted copy of $Q_{k}\to Q_{n}$ . Label $k$ by $A$ if this copy is monochromatic with $A$ and label $k$ by $B$ if this copy is monochromatic with $B$ .

Either the set $\{k\in\mathbb{N}:k\;\text{has label }A\}$ is infinite or else the set $\{k\in\mathbb{N}:k\;\text{has label }B\}$ is infinite. Without loss of generality, suppose that $\{k\in\mathbb{N}:k\;\text{has label }A\}$ is infinite. This implies that for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , $A$ contains a $2$ -distorted copy of the Hamming cube of dimension $k$ .

By an argument of Enflo [15, 16] for any metric space $M^{\prime}$ and any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , every map $f:Q_{k}\to M^{\prime}$ has bi-Lipschitz distortion $\geqslant k^{1-1/p}/T_{p}(M^{\prime})$ . Combining these two observations, we conclude that $T_{p}(A)=\infty$ for all $p>1$ , and hence $p_{A}=1$ . ∎

#### Proposition 9.4 (Failure to decompose into non-positive and non-negative curvature).

For any $D>1$ , there exists a metric space $(M,d)$ (namely the Hamming cube $Q_{N}$ for some $N\in\mathbb{N}$ ) which cannot split as the union of subsets $M=A\cup B$ such that – $A$ embeds into a metric space of non-negative Alexandrov curvature with distortion $\leqslant D$ and – $B$ embeds into a metric space of non-positive Alexandrov curvature with distortion $\leqslant D$ .

#### Proof.

By a theorem of Ohta [37], a metric space of non-negative Alexandrov curvature has BMW type $2$ with constant $1+\sqrt{2}$ . This implies that any map of the Hamming cube of dimension $k$ into a metric space of non-negative Alexandrov curvature has distortion $\geqslant\sqrt{k}/(1+\sqrt{2})$ .

On the other hand, any metric space of non-positive Alexandrov curvature has BMW type $2$ constant $=1$ (the proof essentially goes back to Enflo [15], see e.g. [37]). This implies that any map of the Hamming cube of dimension $k$ into a metric space of non-positive Alexandrov curvature has distortion $\geqslant\sqrt{k}>\sqrt{k}/(1+\sqrt{2})$ .

Find $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\sqrt{k}/(1+\sqrt{2})>D$ . Apply part (A) of Lemma 9.2 to obtain the value $n\in\mathbb{N}$ .

Suppose that the Hamming cube of dimension $n$ can be decomposed as $Q_{n}=A\cup B$ where $A$ embeds into a metric space of non-negative Alexandrov curvature with distortion $\leqslant D$ and $B$ embeds into a metric space of non-positive Alexandrov curvature with distortion $\leqslant D$ . Without loss of generality, the two sets $A$ and $B$ are disjoint. Label each point in $Q_{n}$ by $A$ or by $B$ accordingly. By Lemma 9.2, there exists an isometric embedding $f:Q_{k}\to Q_{n}$ whose image is entirely contained inside $A$ or entirely contained inside $B$ . By our choice of parameters $\sqrt{k}/(1+\sqrt{2})>D$ , we arrive at a contradiction. ∎

#### Proposition 9.5 (A universal metric space cannot be split into two non-universal subspaces).

If $(M,d)$ is a metric space with $M=A\cup B$ for some $A,B\subset M$ and $M$ is universal, then either $A$ is universal or else $B$ is universal.

#### Proof.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ throughout the entire proof.

Since $M$ is universal, for all $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ the $l_{\infty}$ -grid $([m]^{n},||\cdot||_{\infty})$ embeds into $M$ with distortion $<1+\varepsilon$ . Call this embedding $f_{m,n}$ . For each $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ we have a $2$ -coloring of $[m]^{n}$ based on whether a point $\alpha\in[m]^{n}$ has $f(\alpha)\in A$ or $f(\alpha)\in B$ .

Fix $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$ and apply Lemma 9.2 for a sufficiently high $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and the $2$ -coloring of $[m]^{n}$ obtained from $f_{m,n}$ . We conclude that for each $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$ , the $l_{\infty}$ -grid $([m]^{k},||\cdot||_{\infty})$ embeds either to $A$ with distortion $\leqslant 1+\varepsilon$ or to $B$ with distortion $\leqslant 1+\varepsilon$ . We label the pair $(m,k)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ by $A$ or by $B$ accordingly.

Label each $m\in\mathbb{N}$ by $A$ if $\{(m,k)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}:(m,k)\;\text{has label }A\}$ is infinite and label $m\in\mathbb{N}$ by $B$ otherwise. Either $\{m\in\mathbb{N}:m\;\text{has label }A\}$ is infinite or else $\{m\in\mathbb{N}:m\;\text{has label }B\}$ is infinite. Say it is the former. Because for each $m^{\prime}\leqslant m$ and $k^{\prime}\leqslant k$ we have an undistorted embedding $([m^{\prime}]^{k^{\prime}},||\cdot||_{\infty})\to([m]^{k},||\cdot||_{\infty})$ , we conclude for every $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$ , $([m]^{k},||\cdot||_{\infty})$ embeds into $A$ with distortion $\leqslant 1+\varepsilon$ .

By the Fréchet embedding theorem, for every finite metric space $M_{0}$ there exists $k,m$ such that $M_{0}$ embeds into $([m]^{k},||\cdot||_{\infty})$ with distortion $\leqslant 1+\varepsilon$ . Therefore $M_{0}$ embeds into $A$ with distortion $\leqslant(1+\varepsilon)^{2}$ . This shows that $A$ is universal. ∎

## 10. Questions and directions for further study

#### Conjecture 10.1.

There exists $C>0$ such that $\Emb(1,\delta,k)\leqslant e^{Ck}\log 1/\delta$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0<\delta<1$ .

#### Conjecture 10.2.

For each fixed $0<\delta<1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , the power type behavior of $\Emb(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k)$ as $k\to\infty$ is linear, that is:

$$ \limsup_{k\to\infty}\dfrac{\log(\Emb(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k))}{\log k}=\liminf_{k\to\infty}\dfrac{\log(\Emb(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k))}{\log k}=1 $$

#### Question 10.3.

Prove a coloring version of Theorem 1.1 and of Theorem 1.3. How do the bounds change?

#### Question 10.4 (Dependence on the error).

What is the dependence on the bi-Lipschitz error $\varepsilon$ in the path spaces and tree Ramsey problems? Are the upper bounds in Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 sharp up to universal constants? In other words do we have

$$ Path(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k)=e^{\Omega(k\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta))}\;\;\;\text{and}\;\;\;Tree(1+\varepsilon,\delta,k)=e^{\Omega(k\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta))} $$

for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , $0<\delta<1$ and $0<\varepsilon<0.01$ ? What is the dependence when the distortion $C$ is very large? Is it true that for all fixed $C>1$ , $Path(C,\delta,k)$ and $Tree(C,\delta,k)$ grow exponentially in $k$ ?

#### Question 10.5 (Cubes of fixed higher width).

Fix a width parameter $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and an exponent $1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty$ . For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0<\delta<1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , let $N(1+\varepsilon,k,\delta,m,p)$ be the smallest $N$ such that for every subset $\mathcal{D}\subset[m]^{N}$ of size $|\mathcal{D}|\geqslant\delta m^{N}$ there exists a $(1+\varepsilon)$ bi-Lipschitz embedding $f:([m]^{k},||\cdot||_{p})\to(\mathcal{D},||\cdot||_{p})$ . An application of density Hales–Jewett similar to Remark 9.1 shows that $N(1,k,\delta,m,p)<\infty$ . Does the growth of $N(1+\varepsilon,k,\delta,m,p)$ as $k\to\infty$ depend on the choice of width $m$ or exponent $p$ ?

#### Question 10.6 (Grids of fixed higher dimension).

Fix a grid dimension $d\in\mathbb{N}$ . For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0<\delta<1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , let $GRID_{d}(1+\varepsilon,k,\delta)$ be the smallest $N$ such that for all $\mathcal{D}\subset[N]^{d}$ with $|\mathcal{D}|\geqslant\delta N^{d}$ there exists a $(1+\varepsilon)$ bi-Lipschitz map $f:([k]^{d},||\cdot||_{1})\to(\mathcal{D},||\cdot||_{1})$ . A modification of the proof of Theorem 1.2 (with a $4$ -cornered Cantor set for the lower bound) seems to give:

$$ e^{\Omega_{d}(k\log(1/\delta))}\lesssim GRID_{d}(1+\varepsilon,k,\delta)\lesssim e^{O_{d}(k^{d}\varepsilon^{-d}\log(1/\delta))}. $$

For fixed $0<\varepsilon\lesssim 1$ and $0<\delta<1$ , how does $GRID_{d}(1+\varepsilon,k,\delta)$ grow as $k\to\infty$ ?

#### Question 10.7 (Vague Direction).

Find more examples of sequences of finite metric measure spaces $(X_{N},d_{N},\mu_{N})_{N=1}^{\infty}$ with the following property: for every $\delta>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $\mathcal{D}\subset X_{N}$ there exists a metric embedding $f:X_{k}\to\mathcal{D}$ . Here metric embedding can mean either a $(1+\varepsilon)$ bi-Lipschitz map, an undistorted map, or an undistorted map of bounded rescaling. Investigate the dependence of $N$ on the parameters $k$ , $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$ .
